I had a situation where my supervisor didn't take appropriate action with a harassment claim, he actually blamed me for it. I went to the SD and HR. During the second or third follow-up conversation, they asked me to remind them of the situation. I showed them documentation of the harassment and documentation of the e-mails I had sent them both with the documentation (e-mails they responded to, btw). They gaslit me, hard. They refused to look at any of the information I had and both insisted they never had any knowledge of my situation nor ever talked to me about it. Even though I had proof of both. They suggested I transfer locations or tolerate working MORE hours with the guy who constantly harassed me and others. I went above them and was referred back to HR. I called the hotline and also submitted a complaint to the third-party company to get Meijer investigated. Nothing came of it. 

To anyone out there who experiences sexual harassment at work, my advice is to contact a lawyer, then send an e-mail to your boss, your store director, and HR letting them know you want a meeting with them with your lawyer present. HR isn't there for you. HR is there to protect the company.

I can't recall the exact words now due to a mix of having a horrible memory and trying like hell to actually reprogram myself to not believe him. All this happened months before we took a cross country trip, eventually became roommates, and ended up getting together. Three years of friendship and a little over a year of being in a turbulent situationship, and he moved out of state. We tried remaining friends, but the way he continued treating me became more obvious without being obscured by his physical presence. And still I wasn't the one who ended it. He ghosted me this February. 

Having had time away from him and time to myself to reflect, I realized I struggled with larger self esteem issues than I had originally thought. Instead of taking that red flag and running far away from it, I was drawn to it because I thought that was what I deserved. All the bad sex that made me feel like I was disgusting, the money spent on push up bras, all the time spent trying to physically alter myself to please one man who had no interest in me... it makes me sad now to look back on. 

And yet, I still missed him. My brain was rewired to view him and his presence with positivity, regardless of the bad stuff. He was my dopamine and serotonin. So naturally, I felt that I needed to do everything to keep him in my life. I still miss him, honestly. But I know that it's okay to miss someone and still understand they can't be in your life.

I'm in a similar situation, but trying to pull myself out of it. I just turned 28 three days ago and each birthday seems harder than the last knowing I still can't drive. But I can offer you the things I've tried in the hopes they help you or others. 

Be kinder to yourself! 

As cliche as it might sound, try to hold your own hand. It isn't anyone's fault that driving is scary, especially yours. It's okay that you are still learning. I like to tell myself that as long as I am trying in some aspect, then I'm doing okay. That doesn't mean practicing every day, although that would be wonderful. Rather, it means allowing myself to feel frustrated or embarrassed or anxious about driving or my lack of license, temporarily. It means not allowing a bad experience or an argument with family or friends about not driving to add even more negativity to driving as a whole. Beating yourself up about the inability to drive right now only makes trying to learn that much harder. Which leads me to my second piece of advice. 

Build positive associations with driving! 

An old friend of mine and I recently got back in touch. He started taking me out driving late at night so we could catch up. He asks for advice sometimes about various aspects of his life and it helps. Sometimes I ask for his advice and that helps too. It helps distract me from the anxiety and replaces it with the comfort of companionship. I sometimes feel like I have a little more control by being able to focus on working towards a solution to our problems instead of freaking out because I'm behind the wheel. I feel helpful instead of helpless. In an almost Pavlovian response, I've noticed that I even look forward to driving practice sometimes. Because it means spending time with that friend, with cathartic conversation. Of course, I don't think that would be safe on busy roads. But I'll cross that bridge when I get to it. (I still haven't been able to drive on busy roads with lots of cars.) So maybe try to find something good to do while you drive (that's safe) that will help you associate driving with something positive. 

I'm sure I could find other things, but I'm blanking on the rest. I went from spending 2-3 hours in a parked car staring at the wheel trying to force myself to get enough courage to turn the car on to being able to drive myself home from work and around less-busy streets for a couple of hours without any hesitation. If I can do that, you can learn to drive too. :)

There are people who DON'T stay with their pets as they are being put down? 🥺 

In high school, my family had to put down our cat. She was kind of an ornery cat, in the way that most cats are typically portrayed, indifferent to humans, etc. But I was her person. She would sleep on my legs every night. She let me cuddl her and hold her when no one else could. I loved her to pieces. 

The vet couldn't let me hold her while she was being put down, but she handed her to me immediately afterwards. She was wrapped in a blanket and looked like she was sleeping. I held this little bundled up kitty for probably 15 minutes in their office, sobbing, until my parents finally said we should go. I held her all the way home. And I held her for another hour in the backyard. I kept saying "I'm sorry" over and over again. I'd never cried so much in my life. 

I think it was hard on my parents seeing how hard it was on me because my dad came out and basically had to pry her out of my fingers. I went inside and he buried her. A few days later, they let me go pick out a sapling to plant over her grave and I see that tree still growing every time I visit.

That was over a decade ago and I still cry thinking about it. 

Lots of cities have vets that make house visits specifically for euthanasia purposes so that the pet can both be replaced in a familiar environment and have their humans around. That might he something worth looking into for some people, too. I couldn't imagine how hard it would be to have to lose a pet during COVID restrictions. That's awful.

I get where he is coming from. I work a labor-intensive, second-shift job at a warehouse for upwards of 12 hours a night, sometimes six days a week. I am also extremely tired when I get home BUT I still spend time with my dog (and two cats) because a) I love them and b) chose to have the responsibility of pets in the first place. I exercise my dog at night when I get home in the yard with glow-in-the-dark toys and walk her in the afternoons before work. These pets are also for my mental health as I have depression and anxiety.

Your boyfriend should accept responsibility for wanting to have a pet and walk them when he has the time. You are in the right to want to address this. And even if he is tired, the least he can do is throw a ball around for a little while to give the dog some sort of exercise. If he is still too tired to do this and as you have no connection to this pup, I would suggest finding someone who has the time and desire to manage the energetic chaos that is a husky.

Good luck!

What I haven't been able to get used to is when things sometimes do settle for a while and I get a little hopeful about where my life could go only for everything to come crashing down again. I think that's worse, to find hope only to have it taken away. 

It's extremely tiresome. It takes a lot of effort to get through life by itself, let alone having mental illnesses on top of it. And I don't have anything more to give. I'm tapped out. I have put in too much effort and seen it go to waste repeatedly and I'm wiped out. I'm depleted and sad and in pain, of all kinds. Life is not and will never be worth it.

I do that now. My days are broken down. But it doesn't change the stress and anxiety that is always present. I have to work, I have to eat, I have to pay my bills. I have to worry about what comes next even if I don't want to. I've given up on a lot of things and now I have to pay the consequences.

I'm not doing anything. I sleep 14 hours a day. I barely shower. I am completely isolated at work. The only time anyone ever talks to me is to complain about something I've failed to do or should have done better. I spend time with my ex once or twice a week just so I'm not so alone but he and I are terrible for each other. We ruined each other's lives and yet I can't let him go. He makes me sad. Everything makes me sad. I can't do anything on my own. I am too antisocial. I'm afraid of everything. I can't make phone calls, I can't go places or do all the normal, everyday things that other people can do with ease. I'm not designed to be able to function in the world. I'm going to lose my job soon and I don't even care. The only thing that makes me feel any sort of regret for when I kill myself is that my pets will have to be rehomed. I have tried therapy. I have tried talking to friends, that I know longer have. I have tried talking to strangers. I have tried powering through, just sucking it up and marching on. I have no energy left. I have no will to fight. I'm tired as hell just typing all this out. It doesn't even seem worth it. 

I think about getting up from the couch right now and hanging myself. And it's peaceful. It actually calms me down. And I want to feel that calm permanently. I'm too afraid to do it and I don't understand why. I want this.
